## Vocabulary

Terms this pack was harvested with, grouped by their relation to the concept; counts are units matched / sources. Zero-hit terms are listed under Coverage. On every unit line, `keywords:` names the terms that matched.

- **self**: UI/UX design: emerging interactions (101/25)

## Definitions

- [statement] Adaptation is not an unconditional usability improvement. Findlater and Gajos describe mixed evaluation results and usability side effects; Lavie and Meyer find that benefits depend on the task, user population and circumstances of use. (medium confidence) — https://kgajos.seas.harvard.edu/papers/AIMag09-AUIs.pdf · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions · also: http://www.cs.tufts.edu/~jacob/250aui/AdaptiveBenefits_Lavie_IJoHCI10.pdf
- [statement] The MyUI confirmation patterns are not evidence of strict opt-in consent: the described before-adaptation dialogue proceeds if the user accepts or supplies no input before a timeout. A product requiring affirmative acceptance would need a different timeout rule. (low confidence) — https://www.researchgate.net/publication/257998297_User_Control_in_Adaptive_User_Interfaces_for_Accessibility · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] XAUR is a Working Group Note describing user needs and potential requirements; it explicitly says it is not a set of technical requirements developers must strictly follow. Use it to guide design, not as a standalone conformance certificate. (low confidence) — https://www.w3.org/TR/xaur/ · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions

## Structure and components

- [statement] Generative UI changes the response from text in a predefined interface into an interface generated at the time of use, including interactive tools or simulations; Google Research describes this implementation, while Google Cloud distinguishes component selection, declarative descriptions, and open-ended generated code. (medium confidence) — https://research.google/blog/generative-ui-a-rich-custom-visual-interactive-user-experience-for-any-prompt/ · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions · also: https://cloud.google.com/discover/generative-ui, https://www.nngroup.com/articles/generative-ui/
- [statement] Apple advises communicating that AI-generated content may contain errors. This is an uncertainty disclosure recommendation, not a claim that the interface can estimate factual accuracy. (low confidence) — https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/generative-ai · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] The WebXR accessibility explainer says imperative WebGL output does not by itself expose a scene’s structure without external markup, making many automatic accessibility features difficult. Rendering a spatial scene therefore does not by itself establish assistive-technology access. (low confidence) — https://github.com/immersive-web/webxr/blob/main/accessibility-considerations-explainer.md · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions

## How it works

- [statement] The W3C Working Group Note Making Content Usable advises an accessible mechanism to turn off unexpected changes and return to the previous context or settings. This is supplemental design guidance, not a requirement for WCAG conformance. (low confidence) — https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/ · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] As practitioner guidance, FuseLab recommends a nearby action that restores the previous position, plus settings to reset the layout and disable automatic arranging. W3C independently recommends an off mechanism and restoration of prior state. Treat these as design recommendations, not measured evidence that the controls improve retention or trust. (medium confidence) — https://fuselabcreative.com/the-future-of-ai-constructed-design/ · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions · also: https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/
- [statement] AWS recommends approval timeouts, escalation, and a safe fallback, typically blocking the operation, when nobody responds within the defined window. The interface should not leave an unanswered approval waiting indefinitely. (low confidence) — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/agentic-ai-lens/agentsec04-bp02.html · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] AWS recommends retaining who reviewed an approval, when notification and response occurred, which operation was reviewed, the decision, and any escalation events, so the approval history can be reconstructed. (low confidence) — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/agentic-ai-lens/agentsec04-bp02.html · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] Escalation should be a designed recovery path: offer clarification, alternatives or expert intervention for ambiguity, and preserve a resumable plan for human takeover when the agent gets stuck. (medium confidence) — https://www.smashingmagazine.com/2026/02/designing-agentic-ai-practical-ux-patterns/ · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions · also: https://hatchworks.com/blog/ai-agents/agent-ux-patterns/
- [statement] NN/g recommends using AI to draft study questions and documentation, with expert review: generated usability tasks can lead or prime participants even when the prompt includes examples and guidance. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/research-with-ai/ · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] The QualAnalyzer paper demonstrates process traceability by preserving segment-level inputs, instructions and outputs; in its interview-coding case study, classifications and quoted supporting passages make individual coding decisions inspectable. This is a methodological example, not evidence that the software remains publicly installable. (low confidence) — https://arxiv.org/html/2604.03820v1 · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] Google Cloud recommends streaming UI updates to begin rendering while generation continues, because the additional reasoning step affects time to interaction. This is implementation guidance, not a measured guarantee that streaming improves task performance. (low confidence) — https://cloud.google.com/discover/generative-ui · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] In the freehand-gesture study, users with upper-limb impairments could encounter pain and fatigue even when they could perform the gestures; the authors identify index-finger reliance and rigid pinch/grasp thresholds as barriers in the tested implementations. (low confidence) — https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3663547.3746402 · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] Spatial audio needs alternatives: XAUR proposes text descriptions of important audio and a mono option because stereo or binaural soundscapes can hide information from users with one-ear hearing loss or spatial-orientation impairments. (low confidence) — https://www.w3.org/TR/xaur/ · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] For visionOS, Apple recommends keeping controls within the field of view, preferring horizontal layouts, reducing peripheral motion, and minimizing large repetitive gestures. Apple also advises against head-anchored content because it can interfere with Pointer Control. These are platform-specific recommendations. (low confidence) — https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] Expose meaningful objects and action states nonvisually. XAUR proposes spoken menu descriptions on focus; Equal Entry observed that a blind participant could not tell whether an object had been grabbed when no audio notification was provided. (medium confidence) — https://www.w3.org/TR/xaur/ · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions · also: https://equalentry.com/virtual-reality-accessibility-things-learned-from-blind-users/

## How-to and procedures

- [statement] Use AI-generated codes and clusters as a preliminary analysis that researchers inspect and revise. NN/g reports missed transcript sections and inappropriate tags; the QualAnalyzer paper likewise assigns interpretation and the defensibility of findings to the researcher. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/research-with-ai/ · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions · also: https://arxiv.org/html/2604.03820v1

## Problems, failure modes and limitations

- [statement] Control or report adaptive prediction accuracy, predictability and frequency of change. Findlater and Gajos warn that these characteristics can be confounded: changing task distributions to manipulate accuracy may also change other properties of adaptation. Report the algorithm characteristics even when the experiment cannot isolate them. (low confidence) — https://kgajos.seas.harvard.edu/papers/AIMag09-AUIs.pdf · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] Data & Society argues that a pause button alone does not establish meaningful oversight: the user must be able to notice a problem, observe the relevant work and redirect it. Its research agenda also warns that a complete tool-call trace may still fail to explain a strategy change. (low confidence) — https://datasociety.net/research-library/a-sociotechnical-research-agenda-for-the-oversight-of-ai-agents/ · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] Recovery messages should identify completed work, the failed step, and a concrete continuation path. Institute of AI PM recommends distinguishing succeeded, failed, and unattempted steps; Ditto illustrates an upload failure message that explains what succeeded, why the next item failed, whether anything was sent, and how to continue. (medium confidence) — https://www.institutepm.com/knowledge-hub/agentic-ai-ux-patterns · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions · also: https://www.dittowords.com/blog/agentic-ai-content-design
- [statement] For recovery, provide an action history and an available reversal path; when reversal expires, communicate that limit. Smashing Magazine recommends chronological action logs and explicit undo windows; HatchWorks recommends receipts describing changes and rollback options. (medium confidence) — https://www.smashingmagazine.com/2026/02/designing-agentic-ai-practical-ux-patterns/ · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions · also: https://hatchworks.com/blog/ai-agents/agent-ux-patterns/
- [statement] MeasuringU’s review reports mixed empirical alignment: some synthetic results match means, correlations or factor structures, while others show reduced variation, distorted relationships or shallow narratives. Its conclusion is narrower than universal failure: occasional agreement does not yet justify relying on synthetic research for critical decisions. (low confidence) — https://measuringu.com/review-of-experiments-with-synthetic-users/ · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] NN/g recommends AI for drafting research goals, interview or survey questions, test plans, and study documentation, while warning about invented sources and violations of research best practices. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/research-with-ai/ · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] Streak separately reports an invalid generated citation URL that combined parts of two supplied keys and produced a missing-page error. A displayed citation is therefore insufficient evidence of a valid destination in that implementation; its reference-map approach addresses a different problem from visual streaming polish. (low confidence) — https://engineering.streak.com/p/preventing-unstyled-markdown-streaming-ai · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] In her early Vision Pro review, Rebecca Rosenberg reports jumpy targeting of small or distant buttons and says the setting intended to ignore rapid eye movements did not substantially change her experience. This is an individual report, not a general failure rate or a finding about current versions. (low confidence) — https://medium.com/@realrebeccarose/i-have-a-vision-disability-heres-my-early-review-of-apple-vision-pro-2267a2f28c97 · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] Spatial audio needs alternatives: provide text descriptions for important audio and visual indicators for audio-guided actions. Sound alone cannot carry essential interaction information for everyone. (medium confidence) — https://www.w3.org/TR/xaur/ · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions · also: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility

## Comparisons and alternatives

- [statement] An elective adaptation can preserve a stable route through the interface: Findlater and Gajos describe copying predicted items into a separate menu area instead of moving the originals. Users can use the prediction or keep using known locations; checking the prediction still imposes a cognitive cost. (low confidence) — https://kgajos.seas.harvard.edu/papers/AIMag09-AUIs.pdf · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] In the MyUI laboratory study, participants preferred unobtrusive notification with undo when adaptations had large benefits; explicit confirmation before adaptation was more appropriate when the adaptation imposed costs. The authors recommend combining these patterns according to the expected cost and benefit rather than imposing one confirmation pattern everywhere. (low confidence) — https://www.researchgate.net/publication/257998297_User_Control_in_Adaptive_User_Interfaces_for_Accessibility · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] The recent comparative menu study provides bounded evidence rather than a universal menu ranking: it used small tasks and states that its menus do not represent the whole design space. Its authors also caution that EEG findings may not generalize to other populations or tasks and call for replication with more complex menus. (low confidence) — https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0164121225002675 · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] W3C’s cognitive accessibility document provides supplemental guidance rather than additional WCAG conformance requirements. Its personalization recommendations should be described as guidance, not as normative WCAG obligations. (low confidence) — https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/ · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] Before execution, show a readable plan and give users ways to approve it, edit it, or take control. Institute of AI PM also recommends cancellation before execution rather than forcing approval of the whole plan. (medium confidence) — https://www.smashingmagazine.com/2026/02/designing-agentic-ai-practical-ux-patterns/ · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions · also: https://www.institutepm.com/knowledge-hub/agentic-ai-ux-patterns, https://hatchworks.com/blog/ai-agents/agent-ux-patterns/
- [statement] Use risk-tiered approvals rather than sending every action to review. AWS warns that indiscriminate review creates fatigue and rubber-stamp approvals; Smashing Magazine describes different autonomy levels for low-stakes and high-stakes tasks. (medium confidence) — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/agentic-ai-lens/agentsec04-bp02.html · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions · also: https://www.smashingmagazine.com/2026/02/designing-agentic-ai-practical-ux-patterns/, https://datasociety.net/research-library/a-sociotechnical-research-agenda-for-the-oversight-of-ai-agents/
- [statement] When a decision needs human judgment, provide an escalation path instead of silently continuing. Smashing Magazine proposes clarification, choices, and human-expert intervention; AWS calls for escalation when a primary reviewer is unavailable. (medium confidence) — https://www.smashingmagazine.com/2026/02/designing-agentic-ai-practical-ux-patterns/ · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions · also: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/agentic-ai-lens/agentsec04-bp02.html
- [statement] A VS Code issue author reported that an agent created many checkpoints visible in a Git extension and that an attempt to disable checkpoint creation did not help. This is an attributed usability complaint, not proof of present behavior or a released fix. (low confidence) — https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/issues/342038 · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] Make the scope of delegated authority explicit and adjustable: Smashing Magazine recommends autonomy settings per task type, while AWS recommends narrowly scoped, auditable and revocable persistent trust grants rather than wildcard grants. (medium confidence) — https://www.smashingmagazine.com/2026/02/designing-agentic-ai-practical-ux-patterns/ · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions · also: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/agentic-ai-lens/agentsec04-bp02.html
- [statement] AI assistance with study planning and analysis should be distinguished from replacing participants: the former works on research tasks and collected data, while synthetic interviews generate simulated accounts rather than observed human experiences. NN/g recommends supplementing real-user research rather than substituting synthetic users. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/research-with-ai/ · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/synthetic-users/
- [statement] Treat synthetic output as explicitly labeled hypotheses for later human research, rather than presenting it as participant evidence. NN/g recommends hypothesis maps and clear provenance; Synthetic User Council describes its own role as challenging a research brief before real interviews. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/synthetic-users/ · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions · also: https://github.com/kgkazakos/synthetic-user-council/blob/main/docs/WHITEPAPER.md
- [statement] NN/G observed that forced autoscroll during streaming disrupted reading and could make participants wait for completion. It recommends preserving the beginning of a long new response instead of jumping to its end. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/ai-chatbots-design-guidelines/ · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] Redis’s engineering guidance warns that an interrupted or failed stream can appear to be a successful partial answer unless the frontend distinguishes connection loss from an explicit error in the stream. The interaction needs a visible incomplete/error state rather than treating received text as proof of completion. (low confidence) — https://redis.io/blog/streaming-llm-responses/ · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] NN/G’s 2024 generative-UI article anticipates a consistency tradeoff: repeatedly changing layouts can require users to relearn an interface. It presents this as a predicted design challenge, not an observed universal failure of generated interfaces. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/generative-ui/ · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] For uncertainty and failure fallback at the response level, Babich’s practitioner guidance recommends clear expectations, an undo, and a manual fallback for AI features. This remains a design prescription rather than evidence that a specific fallback has been evaluated. (low confidence) — https://agency.uxplanet.org/blog/ai-ux-patterns/ · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] NN/G recommends clickable follow-up suggestions instead of text that users must retype, but also warns against repeating suggestions users have already declined to engage with. This supports progressive exploration without repeatedly prompting the same next step. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/ai-chatbots-design-guidelines/ · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] Apple recommends a non-AI fallback when possible; this is qualified guidance rather than a requirement that every generative feature have a substitute. (low confidence) — https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/generative-ai · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] Provide equivalent ways to complete core interactions rather than requiring a particular gesture: Apple recommends onscreen alternatives to gestures, while XAUR proposes keyboard, switch, speech and eye-tracking input paths. These are design recommendations, not proof that an arbitrary XR application implements them. (medium confidence) — https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions · also: https://www.w3.org/TR/xaur/
- [statement] Provide equivalent ways to perform core actions rather than requiring a particular bodily movement. XAUR proposes access to all interface areas through the same input method; Apple recommends alternatives that achieve the same outcome as gestures. (medium confidence) — https://www.w3.org/TR/xaur/ · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions · also: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility
- [statement] Treat eye tracking as one input option alongside speech, keyboard and switches, rather than as an assumed prerequisite. XAUR describes these input modalities and proposes device-independent actions. This is design guidance, not evidence that every XR platform implements them. (low confidence) — https://www.w3.org/TR/xaur/ · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions

## Facts and statements

- [statement] Findlater and McGrenere distinguish three control models: adaptive interfaces let the system control change; adaptable interfaces let the user control change; mixed-initiative interfaces share control. Personalization should therefore specify who initiates and controls each change. (low confidence) — https://www.cs.ubc.ca/labs/edapt/papers/findlater2004.pdf · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] For disclosure and recovery, expose what changed and provide a way to reject, undo or override it. Peissner and Edlin-White define these as aspects of transparency and controllability; W3C guidance also calls for user-requested changes or an available off switch and a way back to the previous state. (medium confidence) — https://www.researchgate.net/publication/257998297_User_Control_in_Adaptive_User_Interfaces_for_Accessibility · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions · also: https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/
- [statement] Evaluate efficiency and experience separately. Findlater and Gajos recommend task completion time, errors and ratings of obtrusiveness, predictability and usefulness. The comparative adaptive-menu study by Gaspar-Figueiredo and colleagues likewise distinguishes performance from preference and reports that UX and performance measures were not correlated with preference in its experiment. (medium confidence) — https://kgajos.seas.harvard.edu/papers/AIMag09-AUIs.pdf · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions · also: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0164121225002675
- [statement] Test familiar and unfamiliar tasks and allow users to develop expertise. Findlater and Gajos explain that novice and expert users can benefit differently; in Lavie and Meyer’s driving-simulator experiments, fully adaptive behavior helped in familiar situations but increased workload and impaired performance in unfamiliar situations to which the interface had not adapted. These findings do not establish the same effects in every application. (medium confidence) — https://kgajos.seas.harvard.edu/papers/AIMag09-AUIs.pdf · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions · also: http://www.cs.tufts.edu/~jacob/250aui/AdaptiveBenefits_Lavie_IJoHCI10.pdf
- [statement] Assess feature awareness and later task performance alongside immediate efficiency. Findlater and Gajos describe recognition tests for awareness and report that highly accurate adaptations can focus attention on a subset of features, reducing awareness of unused features and impairing performance on new tasks. (low confidence) — https://kgajos.seas.harvard.edu/papers/AIMag09-AUIs.pdf · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] The MyUI findings have explicit limits: participants did not have the actual accessibility impairments being modeled; explanations during the experiment could bias awareness; and the study concentrated on subjective ratings. The authors call for real-world validation, objective performance data and longer-term observation without explicit explanations. (low confidence) — https://www.researchgate.net/publication/257998297_User_Control_in_Adaptive_User_Interfaces_for_Accessibility · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] Keep a stable baseline in evaluations: in Findlater and McGrenere’s split-menu experiment the static menu was significantly faster than the adaptive menu; the adaptable menu was faster than adaptive only under certain conditions, and most participants preferred adaptable. These are results for the tested menus, not proof that adaptation always fails. (low confidence) — https://www.cs.ubc.ca/labs/edapt/papers/findlater2004.pdf · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] W3C cognitive accessibility guidance recommends user initiation or an easy way to disable changes in context, functionality and settings, plus an easy way to return to the previous state. Its pattern explicitly excepts changes essential to the activity. (low confidence) — https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/ · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] Disclose personalization options and make them easy to configure. W3C also recommends permitting rollback to a familiar interface; its route-change example explains the change and its consequences and offers approval or a one-touch return to the original route. (low confidence) — https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/ · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] Evaluate users with relevant expertise and enough exposure to learn the interface. Findlater and Gajos warn that adaptations useful to novices may hinder experts, and that motor and cognitive abilities can change the balance of benefits and costs. (low confidence) — https://kgajos.seas.harvard.edu/papers/AIMag09-AUIs.pdf · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] A negation check also limits the claim that predictability must dominate: the Predictability and accuracy study reports improved satisfaction from both, but accuracy had a stronger effect on performance, utilization and some satisfaction ratings than predictability in its experiment. (low confidence) — https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/1357054.1357252 · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] Smashing Magazine recommends setting agent autonomy per task type, allowing confirmation for one task and pre-approved autonomous action for another. Its example separates scheduling from sending email. (low confidence) — https://www.smashingmagazine.com/2026/02/designing-agentic-ai-practical-ux-patterns/ · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] Approval interfaces should make the proposed action and consequences understandable before consent. AWS calls for relevant data sources and decision context in the approval interface; Institute of AI PM calls for disclosure of affected resources and people. (medium confidence) — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/agentic-ai-lens/agentsec04-bp02.html · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions · also: https://www.institutepm.com/knowledge-hub/agentic-ai-ux-patterns, https://hatchworks.com/blog/ai-agents/agent-ux-patterns/, https://www.smashingmagazine.com/2026/02/designing-agentic-ai-practical-ux-patterns/
- [statement] Show action state in a readable timeline. Institute of AI PM recommends completed, current, and remaining steps; Smashing Magazine recommends indicating whether an action succeeded, is in progress, or was undone. (medium confidence) — https://www.institutepm.com/knowledge-hub/agentic-ai-ux-patterns · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions · also: https://www.smashingmagazine.com/2026/02/designing-agentic-ai-practical-ux-patterns/
- [statement] Institute of AI PM recommends a clear way to check status and pause background work, and real-time visibility that lets users interrupt before consequential tool use. These are practitioner recommendations, not demonstrated cancellation guarantees. (low confidence) — https://www.institutepm.com/knowledge-hub/agentic-ai-ux-patterns · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] A Hermes feature-request author reported being unable to recover deleted or overwritten files and proposed Git-backed snapshots before destructive operations and a rollback command. This establishes a reported recovery need and a proposed remedy, not the current availability of that remedy. (low confidence) — https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/issues/452 · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] Visible progress should distinguish work in progress, successful actions and undone actions; practitioner guidance also recommends a current-step indicator and links to produced artifacts in an activity timeline. (medium confidence) — https://www.smashingmagazine.com/2026/02/designing-agentic-ai-practical-ux-patterns/ · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions · also: https://hatchworks.com/blog/ai-agents/agent-ux-patterns/
- [statement] HatchWorks recommends explicit start, stop, pause and resume controls for asynchronous agents, with defined stop behavior for in-flight tool calls, queued actions, partial completion and rollback messaging. This is design guidance, not evidence that cancelling a task reverses actions already completed. (low confidence) — https://hatchworks.com/blog/ai-agents/agent-ux-patterns/ · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] An audit trail or repeatable model output does not establish correctness. QualAnalyzer warns that consistent coding can systematically diverge from human judgment; MeasuringU similarly reports that correlated synthetic and human responses can still differ systematically. (medium confidence) — https://arxiv.org/html/2604.03820v1 · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions · also: https://measuringu.com/review-of-experiments-with-synthetic-users/
- [statement] In Simulacrum of Stories, Kapania and colleagues interviewed 19 qualitative researchers and asked them to recreate familiar interviews with an LLM probe. Initial narrative resemblance gave way to concerns about contextual depth, ambiguous epistemic position, researcher positionality, participant consent and agency, community erasure, and qualitative research legitimacy. This is evidence about researcher experience and epistemology, not a population-wide accuracy benchmark. (low confidence) — https://dl.acm.org/doi/full/10.1145/3706598.3713220 · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] Synthetic participants can reproduce dominant perspectives while obscuring the people they purport to represent. Kapania and colleagues describe displacement and distortion of community voices; Russell cautions that biased or insufficiently diverse training data can skew simulated insights away from the intended user population. (medium confidence) — https://dl.acm.org/doi/full/10.1145/3706598.3713220 · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions · also: https://interactions.acm.org/archive/view/january-february-2026/the-challenges-of-synthetic-users-in-ux-research
- [statement] Synthetic User Council’s repository whitepaper positions the system as a preparation tool that proposes blind spots, challenged assumptions, interview questions and recruitment priorities. That stated purpose is not independent validation that its simulated personas predict real participants. (low confidence) — https://github.com/kgkazakos/synthetic-user-council/blob/main/docs/WHITEPAPER.md · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] Validity claims must stay tied to the task, population, model, prompt and settings tested. MeasuringU warns that these vary across studies and change over time; Russell calls for validation against real-world human data. A successful replication should not be generalized to untested populations or UX decisions. (medium confidence) — https://measuringu.com/review-of-experiments-with-synthetic-users/ · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions · also: https://interactions.acm.org/archive/view/january-february-2026/the-challenges-of-synthetic-users-in-ux-research
- [statement] Human review must actively examine the data and interpretations. QualAnalyzer warns that preserving prompts and outputs can create an unused audit trail; NN/g recommends checking primary sources and reviewing suggested qualitative codes for misunderstanding. (medium confidence) — https://arxiv.org/html/2604.03820v1 · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/research-with-ai/
- [statement] The Simulacrum of Stories study identifies confirmation-bias and representation risks: researcher-selected persona traits shape responses, and repeated prompting can tune simulated data toward researcher expectations. (low confidence) — https://dl.acm.org/doi/full/10.1145/3706598.3713220 · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] MeasuringU’s review reports mixed results: some synthetic responses correlate with human responses, but reduced variance, incorrect averages or statistical relationships, and shallow narratives can coexist with that apparent agreement. Correlation alone does not establish interchangeability. (low confidence) — https://measuringu.com/review-of-experiments-with-synthetic-users/ · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] QualAnalyzer’s authors distinguish auditability and repeatability from validity: consistent model outputs may still diverge systematically from human judgments, and an audit trail requires active human scrutiny. (low confidence) — https://arxiv.org/html/2604.03820v1 · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] Protocol rehearsal and challenging a research brief are bounded proposed uses for synthetic participants; the Simulacrum study also warns that rehearsal can steer researchers toward model-suggested directions, so these uses do not establish participant replacement validity. (medium confidence) — https://dl.acm.org/doi/full/10.1145/3706598.3713220 · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions · also: https://github.com/kgkazakos/synthetic-user-council/blob/main/docs/WHITEPAPER.md
- [statement] The Synthetic User Council whitepaper explicitly limits its behavioral validation to psychological plausibility, stating that it has not empirically validated its synthetic personas against matched real-user behavior. (low confidence) — https://github.com/kgkazakos/synthetic-user-council/blob/main/docs/WHITEPAPER.md · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] Nielsen Norman Group recommends expanding and collapsing additional product details in place. In its observed Rufus interaction, a More details link instead appended a new chat message, pushing the comparison list out of view; the in-place alternative is a recommendation, not a reported comparative trial result. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/ai-chatbots-design-guidelines/ · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] Streak’s engineering account reports that incomplete Markdown citation links briefly exposed long raw URLs before collapsing to link text. Its constrained-format solution buffered the URL until the link closed, then substituted an application-owned reference mapping and emitted the completed link. (low confidence) — https://engineering.streak.com/p/preventing-unstyled-markdown-streaming-ai · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] Nick Babich’s November 2026 practitioner guidance recommends traceable inline citations that open the source and highlight the passage, and cautions against presenting a bare confidence percentage without explaining where data came from. These are attributed design recommendations, not validated effect sizes. (low confidence) — https://agency.uxplanet.org/blog/ai-ux-patterns/ · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] In assistant-ui issue 1718, a contributor attributed disappearing tool UI to a custom adapter recreating the content array on each chunk, losing previous tool calls. The contributor recommended accumulating tool calls outside the loop; this account does not establish installed release behavior. (low confidence) — https://github.com/assistant-ui/assistant-ui/issues/1718 · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] Google Research’s reported preference evaluation favored generated interfaces over standard LLM formats but explicitly excluded generation speed; it therefore does not establish an end-to-end latency-inclusive advantage. The same report acknowledged occasional output inaccuracies. (low confidence) — https://research.google/blog/generative-ui-a-rich-custom-visual-interactive-user-experience-for-any-prompt/ · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] Streaming needs rendering decisions as well as early output: Google Cloud recommends incremental UI updates for responsiveness, while Streak reports that incomplete streamed Markdown links briefly exposed raw URLs before collapsing into formatted citations. These sources support treating intermediate presentation as a design state. (medium confidence) — https://cloud.google.com/discover/generative-ui · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions · also: https://engineering.streak.com/p/preventing-unstyled-markdown-streaming-ai
- [statement] For source navigation, Streak reports replacing model-generated long citation URLs with short references mapped to original links. This is an implementation report about citation delivery, not evidence that a cited answer is factually correct. (low confidence) — https://engineering.streak.com/p/preventing-unstyled-markdown-streaming-ai · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] Apple’s generative-AI design guidance says specific feedback during generation reduces uncertainty and makes waiting feel purposeful. (low confidence) — https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/generative-ai · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] XAUR treats input changes as a continuity problem: switching devices or interaction modes should preserve task focus and avoid unintended input, and outputs sent to multiple devices need synchronization. (low confidence) — https://www.w3.org/TR/xaur/ · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] The freehand-gesture findings are bounded: the study used the Meta SDK, a limited range of impairments, and short tasks with breaks in one session; its authors call for cross-platform and longer-term investigation. (low confidence) — https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3663547.3746402 · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] The SMA gesture-elicitation study reports that participants favored hand gestures and low physical effort, with choices influenced by task and ability. Its population was VR-experienced people with spinal muscular atrophy, so it does not establish one preferred input for all motor disabilities. (low confidence) — https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.16107 · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] Apple’s visionOS accessibility guidance lists head and hand Pointer Control and Zoom as interaction options. This is platform-specific guidance and does not establish equivalent feature availability on other headsets. (low confidence) — https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] Treat voice as an optional accessible path, alongside other inputs: XAUR proposes voice navigation for users with limited mobility, while Berkeley recommends allowing augmentative and alternative communication device input into XR. (medium confidence) — https://www.w3.org/TR/xaur/ · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions · also: https://udl.berkeley.edu/accessibility/xr-accessibility
- [statement] Make interaction affordances understandable without vision and expose accessibility settings in the contexts where people need them. XAUR calls for discoverable settings across categories; Equal Entry observed blind participants who did not understand the controller ray’s direction and recommended explaining its operation with tactile support. (medium confidence) — https://www.w3.org/TR/xaur/ · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions · also: https://equalentry.com/virtual-reality-accessibility-things-learned-from-blind-users/
- [statement] Nonvisual feedback needs to communicate state and navigation events, not merely add ambient sound. Equal Entry observed missing grab and collision feedback; XAUR proposes spoken menu descriptions on focus and clear visual or audio landmarks. (medium confidence) — https://equalentry.com/virtual-reality-accessibility-things-learned-from-blind-users/ · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions · also: https://www.w3.org/TR/xaur/
- [statement] Comfort belongs in interaction design: Apple recommends minimizing large repetitive gestures and uncontrolled camera motion in visionOS; XAUR calls for alternatives to sickness-triggering interactions and adjustable interaction timing. (medium confidence) — https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions · also: https://www.w3.org/TR/xaur/
- [statement] Evaluate XR interactions with disabled participants during development, and measure comfort as well as successful completion. AbleGamers calls for participation across development stages; the freehand-gesture research found pain and fatigue despite most tasks being completed. (medium confidence) — https://ablegamers.org/thoughts-on-accessibility-and-vr/ · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions · also: https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3663547.3746402
- [statement] In Equal Entry’s blind-user prototype testing, participants had difficulty selecting small objects and keeping focus with controller pointing. The team recommended larger selection areas, but explicitly said the change still required future testing; this is not evidence of a measured improvement. (low confidence) — https://equalentry.com/virtual-reality-accessibility-things-learned-from-blind-users/ · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] Reduce precision and coordination demands: use simple gestures, avoid requiring simultaneous actions, and provide adequately spaced, large interaction targets. (medium confidence) — https://www.w3.org/TR/xaur/ · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions · also: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility
- [statement] Validate target acquisition with blind users. In Equal Entry’s research environment, natural hand movement and missing visual focus confirmation made controller pointing unreliable; the authors recommend larger selection areas. XAUR separately proposes target resizing and sensitivity adjustment. (medium confidence) — https://equalentry.com/virtual-reality-accessibility-things-learned-from-blind-users/ · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions · also: https://www.w3.org/TR/xaur/
- [statement] Task completion alone does not establish comfortable gesture access. In the freehand-gesture study, participants could complete most tasks but still experienced considerable pain, discomfort and fatigue. The study used the Meta SDK, limited impairment coverage, and short tasks with frequent breaks; generalization requires further testing. (low confidence) — https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3663547.3746402 · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions
- [statement] Make spoken descriptions controllable and reduce competing sound. Equal Entry’s participants wanted to stop or skip descriptions and found background audio could obscure announcements; XAUR proposes muting noncritical environmental content. (medium confidence) — https://equalentry.com/virtual-reality-accessibility-things-learned-from-blind-users/ · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions · also: https://www.w3.org/TR/xaur/
- [statement] Make accessibility controls discoverable across relevant contexts, and explain unfamiliar spatial actions. XAUR calls for discoverability beyond a single disability category; Equal Entry found participants did not understand the controller raycast direction and recommended explicit explanation. (medium confidence) — https://www.w3.org/TR/xaur/ · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions · also: https://equalentry.com/virtual-reality-accessibility-things-learned-from-blind-users/
- [statement] Voice access requires usable command targets: XAUR proposes voice-controlled navigation and interaction; Apple advises labeling interface elements appropriately for Voice Control. Neither recommendation establishes support across every headset or application. (medium confidence) — https://www.w3.org/TR/xaur/ · keywords: UI/UX design: emerging interactions · also: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility
